primary.justification: The chapter's entire architecture is organised around how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers — explaining price determination, market types (physical/online, domestic/international), the supply chain (wholesale → retail), the government's regulatory role, and consumer quality assessment. Every named section develops the student's understanding of trade and commerce elements (commodity, production, consumption, capital) and their impact on individual and societal life. Without it the chapter has no purpose.

The section 'Government's Role in the Market' is a dedicated, self-contained section organised entirely around how the government as a political institution regulates markets through four distinct mechanisms: (1) price controls (maximum/minimum prices, minimum wages), (2) quality and safety standards (FSSAI, ISI, BIS approvals), (3) mitigating external effects (pollution regulation), and (4) provision of public goods (parks, roads, policing). The section also grounds this regulatory role in India's ancient tradition via Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right on how political institutions function in the economic sphere.

The Government's Role section analyses how government regulation directly shapes the economic conditions of both buyers (lifesaving drug price caps) and sellers (minimum support price for farmers), and how market failures affect entire communities (pollution regulation). This part of the chapter shows how institutional decisions affect social groups; it is present but not a main focus.

The 'Domestic and International Markets' subsection is a part of the chapter describing how resources (petroleum, diamonds, vegetable oils, software, pharmaceuticals) are distributed across geographies through international trade. The Surat textile market illustrates raw material distribution. It is present in the chapter, but not a main focus.

The Hampi Bazaar section is a part of the chapter established as evidence of India's historically prosperous markets — described as 'the best-provided city in the world' by a Portuguese traveller. The Kauṭilya reference grounds market regulation in India's civilisational wisdom. These are present in the chapter, but not a main focus.
